113.title: The flower
113.hook: why it's fresh; impermanence on a plate
113.howItsDone: Many Hindus place fresh flowers at the home shrine each morning, taking down the previous day's, and often choose flowers or leaves associated with a particular deity, such as hibiscus for Ganesha, lotus for Lakshmi, bilva for Shiva and tulsi for Vishnu or Krishna.

segments.voice: Yesterday, deepa, the lamp. Your line was one flame. Today, something that won't last the day.

Early morning, outside a Hindu temple, in India or in New Jersey. Near the gate, someone is selling flowers: marigolds strung into long orange ropes, jasmine in little bundles, a pile of red hibiscus. They'll all be gone by noon, and by tomorrow they'll be wilted. So why does anyone buy them? Why not a silk flower that lasts a year, dusted once a month? That's the question hiding in the third object on the shelf.
screen: `FLOWER SELLERS AT THE GATE.` → `GONE BY TOMORROW.` → `WHY NOT A SILK ONE?`

segments.voice: The Sanskrit word is pushpa, flower. It's a standard offering in puja, and its small habits tell you what it's for. Flowers are often picked or bought fresh for the morning, and yesterday's are taken down and replaced. One that fell on the ground is usually not offered. And a flower meant for the shrine is often left unsmelled: the first enjoyment of it isn't the giver's. Different forms of the divine have their favorites. Red hibiscus often goes to Ganesha and to the Goddess, the lotus to Lakshmi. For Shiva, people offer the three-part leaf of the bilva tree; for Vishnu and Krishna, a leaf of tulsi, holy basil. And it doesn't have to be grand. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says that when someone offers him a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water with devotion, he accepts it. Four ordinary things; the heart doing the offering is what's weighed. Now the part the flower teaches by itself. Set it down in the morning, and by evening it's drooping. You're offering something that won't last. That's not a flaw. It's honest. Everything on the plate, including the person holding the plate, is on its way somewhere. So you don't offer it once and keep it forever. You do it again tomorrow. Fresh, daily.
screen: `PUSHPA — THE FLOWER.` · `FRESH, NOT SMELLED FIRST.` · `A LEAF, A FLOWER, A FRUIT, WATER.` · `WILTED BY EVENING, SO AGAIN TOMORROW.`

segments.voice: Gently take a flower or a leaf near you, a houseplant, a weed outside, a blossom on the table, or go and look at one where it grows, or picture one, and look closely: the color, the veins, the tiny imperfect edge that won't look like this tomorrow. Set it down somewhere that matters to you, your corner, a windowsill, next to a photo of someone you love. If you pray, you can offer it with a name you honor; then just sit with it.
Pushpa. The flower: offered fresh, left unsmelled, gone by evening, and brought again the next day.
Your line: fresh, daily. What wilts can be offered again. That's day one hundred thirteen.

114.title: The bell
114.howItsDone: Many Hindus ring a small hand bell at the start of puja and during arti, often saying a short traditional verse, and many ring the large bell at a temple's entrance as they walk in.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pushpa, the flower, offered fresh and gone by evening. Your line was fresh, daily.

A teacher walks into a noisy classroom and doesn't shout. She taps a glass with a pen. Ting. And thirty kids look up. A wedding toast works the same way, and so does the chime before a flight announcement. One clean sound, and a room full of scattered attention turns and faces the same way. Hindu homes and temples have known this trick for a very long time. It's the fourth object on the shelf, the small one with the handle, the one you don't just look at. Today: the bell.
screen: `A PEN AGAINST A GLASS.` → `THE WHOLE ROOM LOOKS UP.` → `TODAY: THE BELL.`

segments.voice: The Sanskrit word is ghanta, bell. At home it's usually a small brass hand bell, and on top of the handle you'll often find a little figure: Garuda the eagle for Vishnu's devotees, Nandi the bull for Shiva's, sometimes Hanuman. In temples, bigger bells hang at the entrance, and people ring one as they walk in. Why a bell? People give a few answers, side by side. The first is an invitation. Many priests and families say a short traditional verse as they ring it, asking the gods to come and sending away whatever would get in the way. The bell announces: something is starting. The second is about the room. A sharp, bright ring cuts through the hum of a house, the traffic, the television in the next room. It clears the air the way the pen on the glass did. The third is about you. Ring a good bell and listen: the strike, then a long shimmering tail that fades, and fades. Some people say that fading ring echoes Om, the sound from day two. You can't follow it to its end while you're thinking about your email. So by the time it's gone, you're here. That's why the bell often rings at the start of puja, and again through arti. It isn't decoration. It's how you arrive.
screen: `GHANTA — THE BELL.` · `AN INVITATION: SOMETHING STARTS.` · `A RING THAT CLEARS THE ROOM.` · `FOLLOW IT TO SILENCE: ARRIVE.`

segments.voice: Strike a bell once, gently, or a glass with a spoon, or a singing bowl, or just imagine the sound. Then don't move: follow it as it thins out, all the way down, until you honestly can't tell whether you still hear it. When it's gone, notice where you are, the room, the chair, your breath; you've arrived.
Ghanta. The bell: rung at the start of puja and through arti, to invite, to clear the room, and to bring you all the way here.
Your line: arrive. One ring, followed all the way down, and you're here. Day one hundred fourteen, done.

115.title: The water
115.howItsDone: In puja, many Hindus offer water to the deity as to an honored guest (for the feet, the hands and the mouth), sip a little themselves to purify before beginning, pour water toward the rising sun in the morning, and receive offered water back afterward as a blessing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ghanta, the bell, rung until you've arrived. Your line was arrive.

A guest you love arrives after a long trip. Before the food, before the stories, someone hands them a glass of water and shows them where to wash up. In a lot of homes, that's the host's first move. Now move that same welcome to a small shelf in the corner of a kitchen, and offer it every morning. The last of the five objects is the plainest: usually a small copper or brass cup and a tiny spoon. Today: the water.
screen: `A GUEST ARRIVES.` → `FIRST, A GLASS OF WATER.` → `TODAY: THE WATER.`

segments.voice: In puja, the divine is welcomed like the most honored guest you can imagine, and water does three jobs in that welcome. First, washing. A few drops are offered for the guest's feet, a few for the hands, a few to rinse the mouth, each with its own Sanskrit name, the way you'd offer a traveler a basin. Worshippers often sip a little water themselves at the start, from the palm of the right hand, to be clean before they begin. Second, offering. Water is poured out as a gift. In the morning, some Hindus face the rising sun and pour water from a small pot, watching the stream catch the light. And remember the Gita from two days ago: a leaf, a flower, a fruit, water. Water is on that short list. It costs almost nothing, and it's enough. Third, drinking. After puja, water that has been offered, sometimes mixed with tulsi leaves or used to bathe the image, comes back to the family, a few drops in the palm, sipped. Some homes also keep a little bottle of water from the Ganga, the Ganges, and add a drop. So the same small cup washes, gives and returns. Nothing about it is dramatic. That's the point. The plainest thing on the shelf teaches the plainest lesson: begin clean.
screen: `WELCOMED LIKE AN HONORED GUEST.` · `WASHING: FEET, HANDS, MOUTH.` · `OFFERING: POURED TOWARD THE SUN.` · `DRINKING: IT COMES BACK TO YOU.`

segments.voice: At a sink or with a small cup of water, wash your hands slowly, as if you were getting ready to greet someone important, and feel the water on your fingers. Pour a few drops somewhere as a gift, a houseplant, the soil outside, the cup in your corner; if you pray, you can offer it with a name you honor. Then take one small sip and notice it going down: washed, given, received.
The water. The plainest offering: it washes the honored guest, it's poured out as a gift, and it comes back to be sipped.
Your line: clean. The plainest gift on the shelf is enough. One hundred fifteen days now.

116.title: The sweet
116.howItsDone: Many Hindus place a small portion of food, often a sweet or fruit, before the image at the home shrine as naivedya, wait a few moments, and then share it as prasad with everyone in the house and any guests.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the water: it washes the guest, it is poured out, and it comes back. Your line was clean.

A grandmother is in her kitchen making laddus, little round sweets, for a festival. The grandkids hover. One reaches for the tray, and she swats his hand away, not unkindly. Not yet. First, the shrine. The child sighs, the way children have sighed in that kitchen for generations. Ten minutes later the same tray comes back, and now she presses one into his palm, smiling. Same sweet, same tray. But something happened in those ten minutes, and the children in that house learn it long before they can explain it.
screen: `NOT YET.` → `FIRST, THE SHRINE.` → `THEN, INTO YOUR PALM.`

segments.voice: The Sanskrit word is naivedya: food offered to the divine. It can be a whole meal or a spoonful of sugar crystals, a banana, a cup of milk, a laddu. Sweets are the classic. At home it goes roughly like this. The food is cooked with care, and the cook often doesn't taste it while it's being made for the shrine: the first taste isn't theirs. A little is set before the image on a clean plate, sometimes with a tulsi leaf on top. Water may be sprinkled around it. It sits there a few moments; some families draw a curtain, or simply look away, as if giving a guest privacy to eat. Then the plate comes back, and here's the turn. Once offered, the food isn't naivedya anymore. It's prasad, your word from day twenty-eight: grace, the gift that returns. And prasad is for sharing: with everyone in the house, the guest at the door, the neighbor. People receive it in the right hand, often with a small bow, and try not to refuse it. The Bhagavad Gita puts the idea bluntly: those who eat what remains after an offering are freed from wrong, but those who cook only for themselves eat their own wrongdoing. Food that's kept is just food. Food that's offered and handed round becomes something else. That's what happened in those ten minutes in the kitchen.
screen: `NAIVEDYA — FOOD OFFERED.` · `THE FIRST TASTE ISN'T YOURS.` · `IT RETURNS AS PRASAD.` · `COOK ONLY FOR YOURSELF, AND…`

segments.voice: Set something small to eat in front of you, a piece of fruit, a square of chocolate, a few raisins, and pause before you eat it. If you pray, offer it first to the name you honor; if not, hold it as a gift you didn't make all by yourself: the sun, the farmer, the truck driver. After a few breaths, break it in two if you can, put half aside for someone else, and eat your half slowly.
Naivedya. Food offered to the divine before anyone eats, which comes back as prasad to be shared. Today's word.
Your line: shared. Offered first, then handed round to everyone in the house. See you tomorrow.

117.title: Morning puja
117.hook: the whole thing in four minutes
117.howItsDone: Many Hindu households do a short daily puja at the home shrine in the morning: ringing a bell, lighting a lamp, offering flowers, water and food, saying a mantra or a deity's name, bowing, and sharing the offered food as prasad.

segments.voice: Yesterday, naivedya, the sweet that goes to the shrine first. Your line was shared.

People sometimes imagine puja as a long, complicated ceremony that only a priest can run. At a temple on a festival day, it can be. At home, on a Tuesday, before work, it can be four minutes. This week you've laid out the pieces like parts of a watch: a corner and five objects. One flame, the lamp. A flower, fresh, daily. A bell that helps you arrive. Water: washed, given, received. And a sweet that goes to the shrine first and comes back to be shared. Today, the watch goes together.
screen: `NOT JUST FOR PRIESTS.` → `A WEEK OF PIECES.` → `TODAY: PUT IT TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Puja, your word from day eight, means honoring, worship, and that day's line still holds: attention is an offering. Full temple worship can have sixteen services, the whole welcome of a royal guest. Many homes use a short form, and old manuals even name a five-part version: fragrance, flower, incense, lamp and food. Your week covered three of those five, the flower, the lamp and the food, and added a bell and water. So here's one simple morning shape. Families do it in different orders, and none is the only right one. Begin clean: wash, or sip a little water. Ring the bell, and let it bring you here. Light the lamp. Offer a flower and a few drops of water. Set down something sweet. Then the heart of it: a few moments of mantra, Om, or the one from the mantra days that fits you, Om namah shivaya or the Gayatri, or simply the name you honor, said quietly. Then pranam, the bow from day four: hands together, head down. Last, take a little of the sweet back as prasad, and share the rest later. Bell, lamp, flower, water, food, name, bow. Some mornings you'll do all of it. Some mornings you'll just light the lamp and bow, and that small version is attention given too. The point was never the full list. The point is that before the day grabs you, something else gets the first four minutes.
screen: `PUJA — ATTENTION IS AN OFFERING.` · `A FIVE-PART FORM FOR HOME.` · `BELL, LAMP, FLOWER, WATER, FOOD.` · `A NAME, A BOW, THE SWEET RETURNS.`

segments.voice: However small your corner is, even if it's only in your mind, go through it once: ring the bell or tap a glass and listen until it fades, light the lamp or picture it, then set down a flower or a leaf, a few drops of water and a small piece of something sweet. Quietly say your mantra or a name you honor a few times, if you'd like. Then put your hands together, bow, and sit in front of it for the rest of the time.
Morning puja. The home shrine, put together: bell, lamp, flower, water, food, a name and a bow, before the day begins. Today's word.
Your line: four minutes. Any version of it counts, even a lamp and a bow. Day one hundred seventeen, and that's the week.

118.title: The hour
118.hook: the three junctions of the day
118.howItsDone: Traditionally, sandhyavandana, a prayer centered on the Gayatri mantra, is said at dawn, noon and dusk, especially by those who wear the sacred thread; in many Hindu homes, a lamp is lit at dusk and the household pauses as it's lit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, morning puja: bell, lamp, flower, water, food, a name and a bow. Your line was four minutes.

There's a moment on a summer evening when the streetlights haven't come on yet, but the sky has stopped being day. The colors go strange. The birds get loud, then quiet. Someone on a porch says, look at that, and nobody answers, because everyone's looking. Photographers call it the golden hour, and the blue hour after it. A new week starts today, the week of sunset and arti, and it opens with a question: when?
screen: `NOT DAY, NOT YET NIGHT.` → `A NEW WEEK: SUNSET AND ARTI.` → `TODAY: THE HOUR.`

segments.voice: The Sanskrit word is sandhya, from a word for joining: a junction, the place where two things meet. So sandhya means twilight, and more than that: the joints of the day. Tradition names three. Dawn, where night meets day. Noon, where morning turns into afternoon. Dusk, where day meets night. These are the hours set aside for prayer. A whole ancient practice is named for them, sandhyavandana, honoring the junctions, and at its heart is the Gayatri, your mantra from day one hundred eight, a prayer to the light of the sun. Traditionally it's kept by those who wear the sacred thread, and other Hindus keep a simpler version of the idea. Why the junctions? People explain it a few ways. A junction belongs to neither side, so it's a natural doorway, a gap in the ordinary. The light is changing, and when the light changes, people notice. And practically, dawn and dusk are when a busy household stops anyway: before the day's work, and after it. So at home, dusk often has its own small rite. Someone lights the evening lamp as the sun goes down, and in some families people stop what they're doing when it's lit, even for a moment. The day is being handed over to the night, and someone should be there for it.
screen: `SANDHYA — A JOINING, A JUNCTION.` · `DAWN, NOON, DUSK.` · `SANDHYAVANDANA AND THE GAYATRI.` · `THE EVENING LAMP AT SUNSET.`

segments.voice: If it's near dawn or dusk, find a window or step outside; if it isn't, remember the last sunset you really watched. Look at the light itself, not at anything in particular, and notice that it's changing even as you watch; nothing is asked of you but to be present at the joining. If you pray, this is one of the hours tradition sets aside; if not, simply be the one who noticed the day turning.
Sandhya. A joining: the twilight, and the three junctions of the day, dawn, noon and dusk, set aside for prayer. Today's word.
Your line: the junction. Where two things meet, there's a doorway in the ordinary. One hundred eighteen days in.

119.title: Arti at home
119.howItsDone: At home, many Hindus perform arti at dawn and at dusk by circling a small ghee lamp or burning camphor clockwise before the image, often in a pattern from the feet to the face, while a bell is rung and an arti song is sung.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sandhya, the hour where two things join. Your line was the junction.

On the banks of the Ganga at dusk, priests stand in a row, each holding up a huge brass lamp with a crown of flames, swinging it in slow circles as bells clang and thousands of people sing. The river turns gold. It's one of the most famous sights in India, and maybe you've seen it in videos. Now shrink it. A kitchen. A shelf. One small plate with one small flame, held by someone in socks, and maybe a kid ringing a bell a little too hard. Same act.
screen: `THE GANGA AT DUSK, LAMPS BLAZING.` → `NOW SHRINK IT.` → `ONE PLATE, ONE FLAME, AT HOME.`

segments.voice: Arti was your fourteenth word, way back in camp one: light passed hand to hand. That was what it means; today is how it's done. The word comes from the Sanskrit aratrika, often explained as a rite done at night, or one that removes darkness. At home, the lamp is usually a small plate with a ghee wick, or a piece of camphor that burns bright and fast. You stand before the image and move the flame in slow circles, clockwise. Many people make a pattern: a few circles at the feet, a few at the middle, a few at the face, then around the whole form. Families do it in different ways, and there's no single count everyone agrees on. While the flame circles, a bell rings, in your other hand or someone else's. And there's singing: an arti song, which you'll learn tomorrow. Why circle? People give a few answers. You circle what's at the center of your life, so a flame circled before the image puts the divine at the center. It also lets the light fall on every part of the form, as if you were seeing all of it by lamplight. And people often point out that camphor burns without leaving any ash behind. Some say that's the whole hope of devotion: burn bright, give light, and leave no ego behind.
screen: `ARTI — FROM ARATRIKA.` · `A SMALL FLAME, CIRCLED CLOCKWISE.` · `FEET, MIDDLE, FACE, THE WHOLE.` · `CAMPHOR LEAVES NO ASH.`

segments.voice: If you have a candle or small lamp and it's safe, light it and hold it steady on a plate in your right hand; if not, use your open hand, or just your eyes. Before an image, a photo or simply a window, make a few slow circles clockwise, a few low, a few in the middle, a few at the height of a face, slowly enough to watch the light move. Then set it down and sit with the flame.
Camphor, the flame that burns bright and leaves no ash: circled clockwise at home in front of the image, with a bell and a song, so the light falls on every part. Today's word.
Your line: light, circled. What you circle, you put at the center. That's day one hundred nineteen.

fork.setup: you're holding the arti flame in front of the image for the first time. which way do you circle it?
fork.reveal: clockwise. circling keeps the divine at the center, and many families move from the feet to the face to the whole form.

original.note: Hindi ārtī, from Sanskrit ārātrika: the rite of the circled lamp.

trapdoor: what you thought: waving a candle around.
what it means: a flame circled clockwise before the image, with a bell and a song, so the light falls on every part of the form.
what a scholar hears: arti derives from ārātrika, variously explained as a nighttime rite or as the removal of darkness; camphor's residue-free burning is a common image for the dissolving of ego.
